lesson.title: Power of a Power, and the Zero Exponent
lesson.subject: math

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you multiplied and divided powers. Today: what happens when you raise a power to another power!

When raising a power to another power, multiply the exponents: (x³)⁴ = x¹² (since it means x³ multiplied by itself 4 times, giving 3+3+3+3=12 total factors of x). Any nonzero number raised to the power of 0 equals 1: x⁰ = 1 — this follows from the quotient rule, since x³/x³ = x⁰ but also clearly equals 1. Simplify (x²)⁵ and evaluate 7⁰.
You just learned the power-of-a-power and zero-exponent rules! Tomorrow we'll learn what negative exponents really mean.

objectives: State the power-of-a-power rule: multiply exponents
State that any nonzero number to the power of 0 equals 1, and explain why using the quotient rule
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's product/quotient rules briefly.
2. Introduce the power-of-a-power rule, expanding (x³)⁴ by hand to show why it works.
3. Introduce the zero-exponent rule using the x³/x³ = x⁰ = 1 reasoning.
4. Have the child simplify (x²)⁵ and evaluate 7⁰.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's negative-exponents lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: physically expand (x²)³ into (x·x)(x·x)(x·x) before introducing the shortcut rule
Ready for more: ask the child to prove x⁰=1 a second way, using a pattern like x³, x², x¹, x⁰ and noticing each step divides by x
The zero-exponent rule often feels arbitrary to students — grounding it in the quotient rule (rather than just stating it) makes it feel earned, not memorized
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Algebra 1 standards on properties of exponents, continuing this week's thread with the power-of-a-power and zero-exponent rules.
